Acceptance summary:

There is broad interest in diseases related to loss of lysosome acidification, and your studies on the link between this process and cellular iron regulation have important implications for our understanding of the etiology of a number of disease processes and the links between lysosome and mitochondrial function and inflammatory signaling.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Impaired lysosomal acidification triggers iron deficiency, necrotic cell death and inflammation in vivo" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Suzanne Pfeffer as the Reviewing and Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Peter S McPherson (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

In this manuscript Raimundo and colleagues investigate how inhibition of lysosomal acidification impacts cellular iron homeostasis, inflammation and cell death. The authors pursue mechanistic studies in cultured cells, before moving into an in vivo model of lysosome dysfunction, and develop a model that links lysosome de-acidification to cytosolic iron deficiency, inflammatory gene expression and motor dysfunction. This is a well-written manuscript that presents a number of interesting findings in a clear and logical manner.

Before publication can be recommended, the following issues need to be addressed to ensure that the small molecule reagents you have employed are consistent with the conclusions of your study.

1) Bafilomycin A is used to study loss of lysosomal acidification. To ensure that this is the case (as opposed to an unrelated effect of v-ATPase inhibition), compounds that dissipate or clamp lysosomal pH in an vATPase-independent manner (i.e. chloroquine) should be tested; Also, there are some concerns about the concentration of Baf used. 500nM is much higher than the IC50, which is in the low nanomolar. To rule out indirect effects, it would be important to carry out RNAi of an essential vATPase subunit and determine whether it also results in activation of the hypoxic response and disrupted mitochondrial function.

2) The authors imply that v-ATPase inhibition results in build-up of iron in the lysosome. Whole-cell measurements of iron levels show a decrease in both Fe2+ and Fe3+ following Baf treatment (Figure 1E). However, if iron is trapped in lysosomes, the expectation is that its subcellular distribution should be altered, not its total concentrations. The authors could repeat the iron measurements described in the Materials and methods after fractionating the cells to separate light organelle fraction from cytosol (an easy procedure that should confirm reduced cytosolic iron levels), or upon lysosomal immunoprecipitation (i.e. PMID: 29074583). If iron accumulation within lysosomes is the ultimate cause of the observed mitochondrial dysfunction, this phenotype should be recapitulated by ablation of the main iron-exporting permeases, SLC11A2 and MCOLN1, either individually or in combination.

3) An alternative explanation for the observed mitochondrial dysfunction in Baf-treated cells is impairment of mitophagy. Are Baf-dependent induction of the hypoxic response and mitochondrial dysfunction identical between wild-type cells and cells lacking essential autophagic factors (i.e. Atg7)?

4) The authors use a RIPK-1 inhibitor, known as necrostatin, to imply a role for necroptosis in Baf-induced cell death. It should be noted that the specificity of action of necrostatin is questionable (i.e. https://doi.org/10.1038/cddis.2012.176), thus it is highly recommended that the authors further support this conclusion with RNAi-based experiments. Demonstration that the cell death process is necroptosis may be beyond the scope of the present story and could be removed.

5) The GAA-defective cells and mice are assumed, but not shown, to have defective lysosomal acidification. Given the importance of this assumption for their model, the authors should re-check it on their own at least in the cell model. Also, GAA loss has more ample consequences than just loss of lysosomal acidity. This caveat should be acknowledged and adequately discussed.

claims.claim: Bafilomycin treatment results in halting of cell proliferation and cell death in fibroblasts.
claims.source: We observed that fibroblasts treated with vehicle control proliferate, while both bafilomycin (Figure 4A) and saliphe treatments (Figure 4B) resulted not only in halting of cell proliferation but also in cell death (the number of cells decreases during the treatment).

claims.source: We observed that fibroblasts treated with vehicle control proliferate, while both bafilomycin (Figure 4A) and saliphe treatments (Figure 4B) resulted not only in halting of cell proliferation but also in cell death (the number of cells decreases during the treatment).

claims.claim: Fe-citrate supplementation restores cellular proliferation in v-ATPase inhibitor-treated fibroblasts.

claims.claim: Antimycin A treatment ablates the recovery in cell viability conferred by iron supplementation in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.

claims.evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation and antimycin A treatment (Figure 4D).

claims.evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation and antimycin A treatment (Figure 4E).

claims.claim: Antimycin A treatment ablates the recovery in cell viability conferred by iron supplementation in deferoxamine-treated fibroblasts.

claims.claim: Bafilomycin-induced cell death is not apoptotic as shown by absence of cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP.
claims.source: We could not detect either cleaved caspase-3 or cleaved PARP in bafilomycin- (Figure 4F) or saliphe-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), despite they were readily detectable in cells treated with the apoptosis inducer staurosporine.
claims.evidence: Shown by immunoblots of cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4F).

claims.evidence: Shown by immunoblots of cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP in saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claims.claim: Pan-caspase inhibitor ZVAD has no attenuating effect on cell death in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts.

claims.claim: Necrostatin-1s has no effect on cell death caused by v-ATPase inhibition.

claims.evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in bafilomycin-treated fibroblasts with necrostatin-1s treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).

claims.claim: Ferrostatin has no effect on v-ATPase inhibition-induced cell death.

claims.evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in bafilomycin or saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts with ferrostatin treatment (Figure 4H).

claims.claim: Deferoxamine treatment results in increased Tnfa expression in primary cortical neurons.

claims.evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tnfa in deferoxamine-treated primary neurons (Figure 4I).

claims.claim: Deferoxamine treatment results in increased expression of innate immune regulators in primary cortical neurons.

claims.evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tlr9, Myd88, Irf7, Stat1, and Stat2 in deferoxamine-treated primary neurons (Figure 4J).

claims.claim: Deferoxamine treatment results in increased expression of interferon-stimulated genes in primary cortical neurons.

claims.claim: Gaa-KO mouse cortex shows increased Tfrc transcript levels at 6 and 12 months of age.

claims.evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of Tfrc in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 6 and 12 months (Figure 5A).

claims.claim: Gaa-KO mouse cortex shows decreased FTL1 protein levels at 6 and 12 months of age.

claims.claim: Gaa-KO mouse cortex shows increased HIF-1α protein levels at 6 and 12 months of age.

claims.evidence: Shown by immunoblots of HIF-1α in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 6 and 12 months (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: Gaa-KO mouse cortex shows decreased complex IV activity.

claims.evidence: Shown by native complex IV activity staining in mitochondria purified from Gaa-KO mouse cortex (Figure 5D).

claims.claim: Gaa-KO mouse brain shows decreased T2 relaxation time of water protons in thalamus, striatum, and cerebral cortex.
claims.source: For this, we analyzed the thalamus, striatum and cerebral cortex, and in all three regions we found a decrease in the T2 relaxation time of water protons (Table 1), which is highly correlated with reduced labile iron pool levels (Vymazal et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: Shown by MRI measurements in Gaa-KO mice at 6 and 12 months (Table 1).

claims.claim: Gaa-KO mouse brain shows reduced levels of choline-containing compounds by MRS.

claims.evidence: Shown by MRS measurements in Gaa-KO mice at 6 and 12 months (Figure 5E-F).

claims.evidence: Shown by immunoblots of PLP and MBP in Gaa-KO mouse cortex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).

claims.claim: RNA sequencing of Gaa-KO mouse cortex identified 1779 differentially expressed genes.

claims.evidence: Shown by RNA sequencing analysis of Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 12 months.

claims.claim: The most significantly changed transcripts in Gaa-KO cortex include Gaa and proteins related to immune responses.

claims.evidence: Shown by RNA sequencing analysis of Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 12 months (Figure 6B).

claims.claim: Several pathways related to inflammation are enriched in the Gaa-KO cortex dataset.

claims.evidence: Shown by pathway analysis of RNA sequencing data from Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 12 months (Figure 6C).

claims.claim: Irf7 and Irf3 are predicted as the two most active transcription factors in Gaa-KO cortex.

claims.evidence: Shown by upstream regulator analysis of RNA sequencing data from Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 12 months (Figure 6D).

claims.claim: 17 out of 20 Irf7 targets are robustly up-regulated in Gaa-KO cortex.

claims.evidence: Shown by analysis of Irf7 target genes in RNA sequencing data from Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 12 months (Figure 6E).

claims.claim: Most interferon-stimulated genes and their regulators are up-regulated in Gaa-KO cortex at 2, 6, and 12 months of age.

claims.evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of interferon-stimulated genes in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 2, 6, and 12 months (Figure 6F).

claims.claim: Stat1 is up-regulated only at 12 months in Gaa-KO cortex.

claims.claim: Gaa-KO cortex shows increased GFAP protein levels at 6 and 12 months of age.

claims.evidence: Shown by immunoblots of GFAP in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 6 and 12 months (Figure 6G).

claims.claim: Gaa-KO cortex shows increased number of GFAP-positive cells at 6 months of age.

claims.evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence staining of GFAP in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 6 months (Figure 6H).

claims.claim: Tfam transcript levels are only 20% down in Gaa-KO brain.

claims.source: Therefore, we supplemented the cell medium with Fe-citrate, and observed that the mtDNA copy number increased in iron-supplemented Gaa-KO fibroblasts to control values (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of mtDNA copy number in Gaa-KO fibroblasts with Fe-citrate supplementation (Figure 7C).

claims.claim: Iron-enriched diet rescues mtDNA copy number defects in 2-month-old Gaa-KO mice.
claims.source: While the GAA-KO mice treated with the control Na-citrate diet showed a ~ 20% decrease in mtDNA in cortex relative to the WT littermates, the Gaa-KO cohort fed iron-enriched chow had mtDNA copy number similar to the WT mice (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of mtDNA copy number in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 2 months with iron-enriched diet (Figure 7D).

claims.claim: Iron-enriched diet dampens increased expression of innate immune response genes in 2-month-old Gaa-KO mice.
claims.source: So, we analyzed the transcript levels of interferon-stimulated genes and those of their regulators in the cortex of 2 month old mice in Fe-enriched or control diet, and observed that in the iron-supplemented Gaa-KO mice the inflammatory response was ablated (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: Shown by qPCR measurements of interferon-stimulated genes in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 2 months with iron-enriched diet (Figure 7E).

claims.claim: Iron-enriched diet decreases GFAP and TNFα protein levels in 2-month-old Gaa-KO cortex.
claims.source: Furthermore, we observed that the protein levels of GFAP and of the inflammatory mediator TNFα were also decreased by the iron-supplementation in the Gaa-KO cortex (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Shown by immunoblots of GFAP and TNFα in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 2 months with iron-enriched diet (Figure 7F).

claims.claim: Iron-enriched diet normalizes cytokine levels in 2-month-old Gaa-KO cortex.
claims.source: While we barely could observe TNFα, interferon gamma (IFNγ) as well as the cytokines CXCL9, CXCL10, CXCL11, IL-1α, IL-16 in wild type mice, these proteins were significantly increased in the cortices of Gaa-KO fed standard chow, but were normalized to the barely detectable WT levels in the iron-supplemented mice (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: Shown by cytokine array measurements in Gaa-KO mouse cortex at 2 months with iron-enriched diet (Figure 7G).

claims.claim: Iron-enriched diet normalizes stride length in 2-month-old Gaa-KO mice.
claims.source: We observed that several parameters were affected in the Gaa-KO already at 2 months of age, particularly the stride length, which was decreased in the Gaa-KO mice (Figure 7H). This is an indication of gait disorder (Fernagut et al., 2002), suggesting that the Gaa-KO mice may have motor impairments. Notably, the Gaa-KO mice supplemented with iron showed a normalization of the stride length (Figure 7H).
claims.evidence: Shown by DigiGait analysis in Gaa-KO mice at 2 months with iron-enriched diet (Figure 7H).

claims.claim: Decreased stride length in Gaa-KO mice is an indication of gait disorder.
claims.source: This is an indication of gait disorder (Fernagut et al., 2002), suggesting that the Gaa-KO mice may have motor impairments.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Fernagut et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Impaired lysosomal acidification links to mitochondrial malfunction and inflammation in vivo.
claims.source: Our results highlight a novel mechanism linking impaired lysosomal acidification, mitochondrial malfunction and inflammation in vivo.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by the comprehensive data showing iron deficiency, mitochondrial dysfunction, mtDNA instability, and inflammation in Gaa-KO mice, all corrected by iron supplementation.

claims.claim: Iron release from (endo)lysosomes to cytoplasm requires acidic pH.
claims.source: We show here that iron release from (endo)lysosomes to cytoplasm requires acidic pH.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by increased lysosomal iron and decreased cytoplasmic iron in bafilomycin-treated cells (Figure 1F, I).

claims.claim: Fe3+ obtained from ferritinophagy, mitophagy or transferrin endocytosis cannot be reduced to Fe2+ when lysosomes are not properly acidified.
claims.source: When the (endo)lysosomes are not properly acidified, Fe3+ obtained from ferritinophagy, mitophagy or transferrin endocytosis cannot be reduced to Fe2+.
claims.evidence: Based on the known function of STEAP3 requiring acidic pH and the observed accumulation of Fe3+ in Gaa-KO fibroblasts (Figure 2I).

claims.claim: STEAP3 has an optimal acidic pH for Fe3+ reduction.
claims.source: This reduction is catalyzed by the ferroreductase STEAP3, which has an optimal acidic pH (Lambe et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Lambe et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Only Fe2+ can be exported from lysosomes via DMT1 or MCOLN1.
claims.source: The inability to reduce Fe3+ to Fe2+ results in the accumulation of Fe3+ in the lysosomes, since only Fe2+ can be exported via the channels divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) or mucolipin-1 (MCOLN1) (Dong et al., 2008; Touret et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2008 and Touret et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Cytoplasmic Fe levels determine when the cellular iron deficiency response is activated.
claims.source: The proteins that sense cellular iron function are located in the cytoplasm, implying that cytoplasmic Fe levels determine when the cellular iron deficiency response is activated.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of IRP1 and IRP2 function in the cytoplasm.

claims.claim: Low Fe levels result in the conversion of aconitase in IRP1 and stabilization of IRP2.
claims.source: Low Fe levels result in the conversion of aconitase in IRP1 and stabilization of IRP2 (Rouault, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Rouault, 2015.

claims.claim: IRP1 and IRP2 promote iron mobilization and uptake while repressing storage and export.
claims.source: Together, these proteins promote iron mobilization and uptake, while repressing its storage and export from the cell.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of IRP function.

claims.claim: The iron homeostatic program requires functional lysosomes.
claims.source: We show here that this program of iron homeostasis requires functional lysosomes.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by iron deficiency response in cells with impaired lysosomal acidification.

claims.claim: Iron deficiency caused by v-ATPase inhibition results in cell death.
claims.source: Accordingly, inhibition of lysosomal v-ATPase and the consequent iron deficiency result in cell death.
claims.evidence: Shown by cell viability assays in bafilomycin or saliphenylhalamide-treated fibroblasts (Figure 4A-B).

claims.claim: The main contributor to cell death caused by impaired lysosomal acidification is iron deficiency.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the simple repletion of iron through an (endo)lysosome-independent pathway was sufficient to restore cell proliferation almost to control levels. Therefore, the main contributor to cell death caused by impaired (endo)lysosomal acidification seems to be iron deficiency.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by Fe-citrate supplementation restoring cell viability in v-ATPase inhibitor-treated cells (Figure 4C).

claims.claim: The cell death caused by iron deficiency is non-apoptotic and likely contributes to inflammation in vivo.
claims.source: We determined that the cell death caused by iron deficiency is non-apoptotic, which likely contributes to the inflammation observed in vivo in the brain of a mouse model of lysosomal malfunction (Gaa-KO).
claims.evidence: Shown by absence of apoptotic markers in bafilomycin-treated cells (Figure 4F-G) and inflammation in Gaa-KO brain (Figure 6).

claims.claim: The inflammation trigger caused by iron deficiency is cell-intrinsic.
claims.source: While we cannot exclude the possibility that neuronal cell death in culture was sensed by astrocytes or glia that are present in the culture (primary neurons typically have a small number of co-cultured astrocytes and microglia), our results suggest that the inflammation trigger is cell-intrinsic.
claims.evidence: Suggested by increased inflammatory gene expression in deferoxamine-treated primary neurons (Figure 4I-K).

claims.claim: mtDNA replication relies mostly on cytoplasmic dNTP production.
claims.source: There is no dedicated de novo production of dNTPs for mtDNA synthesis, and mtDNA replication relies mostly on the cytoplasmic dNTP production (Copeland, 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Copeland, 2012.

claims.claim: Ribonucleotide reductase has Fe in its active center.
claims.source: A key step in dNTP production is catalyzed by the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase, a heterodimeric protein that has Fe in its active center (Puig et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Puig et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Decreased availability of dNTPs is a known cause of mtDNA instability.
claims.source: Decreased availability of dNTPs is a known cause of mtDNA instability, which in turn is an inflammatory trigger.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Iron deficiency perturbs mtDNA homeostasis regardless of cell type or mechanism.
claims.source: We show here that iron deficiency perturbs mtDNA homeostasis, regardless of the cell type (fibroblasts, neurons) or the mechanism (genetic, pharmacologic) that leads to iron deficiency.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by decreased mtDNA in deferoxamine-treated cells, Irp1/2-KO cells, and Gaa-KO cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-E).

claims.claim: The levels of mtDNA decrease sharply in iron deficiency.
claims.source: We also show here that the levels of mtDNA decrease sharply in iron deficiency.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by decreased mtDNA in various iron deficiency models (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-E).

claims.claim: In Tfam+/- mice, mtDNA instability triggers interferon-dependent signaling that culminates in potent inflammatory responses.
claims.source: In the Tfam+/- mice, mtDNA instability triggers interferon-dependent signaling that culminates in potent inflammatory responses (West et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to West et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Iron deficiency is associated with mtDNA instability and inflammation in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: We show here that iron deficiency, either caused by iron chelation, genetic ablation of Irp1 or Irp2, or genetic defects impairing lysosomal acidification, is associated both with mtDNA instability and inflammation, in vitro and, importantly, in vivo.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by decreased mtDNA and increased inflammatory markers in various iron deficiency models (Figures 6, 7).

claims.claim: Supplying iron via an endo/lysosome-independent route resolves iron deficiency response, loss of mtDNA, and inflammatory signaling.
claims.source: Notably, supplying iron via an endo/lysosome-independent route resolved the iron deficiency response, the loss of mtDNA and the inflammatory signaling.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by Fe-citrate supplementation rescuing these phenotypes in cells and iron-enriched diet rescuing them in mice (Figures 2-4, 7).

claims.claim: Prolyl hydroxylases catalyze the hydroxylation of HIF-1α.
claims.source: The prolyl hydroxylases are part of the α-ketoglutarate-dependent superfamily, and catalyze the hydroxylation of the α-subunit of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1α).
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of HIF-1α regulation.

claims.claim: After hydroxylation, HIF-1α is recognized by VHL and labeled for proteasomal degradation.
claims.source: After hydroxylation, HIF-1α is recognized by the ubiquitin ligase VHL, and labeled for proteasomal degradation (Raimundo et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Raimundo et al., 2011.

claims.claim: HIF-1α is constitutively expressed and readily degraded under normal conditions.
claims.source: HIF-1α is therefore constitutively expressed and readily degraded under normal conditions, and thus barely detectable (Raimundo et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Raimundo et al., 2011.

claims.claim: In the absence of VHL or when prolyl hydroxylases are impaired, HIF-1α accumulates and triggers the pseudo-hypoxia response.
claims.source: However, in the absence of VHL or when the function of prolyl hydroxylases is impaired, HIF-1α accumulates and triggers a transcriptional program known as (pseudo-)hypoxia response.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of HIF-1α regulation.

claims.claim: Activation of HIF signaling is a consequence of impaired lysosomal acidification.
claims.source: Therefore, the activation of HIF signaling is a novel consequence of impaired lysosomal acidification (Miles et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Miles et al., 2017 and data showing HIF-1α accumulation in v-ATPase inhibitor-treated cells (Figure 1D).

claims.claim: HIF signaling can be activated by mitochondrial malfunction, particularly loss-of-function of fumarate hydratase or succinate dehydrogenase.
claims.source: Notably, HIF signaling can also be activated by mitochondrial malfunction, particularly loss-of-function of the citrate cycle enzymes fumarate hydratase or succinate dehydrogenase, which results in the accumulation of fumarate and succinate, and in the consequent inhibition of the prolyl hydroxylases.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: HIF-1α can be seen as a sensor of the mitochondrial-lysosomal axis.
claims.source: Therefore, HIF-1α can be seen as a sensor of the mitochondrial-lysosomal axis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the data showing HIF-1α accumulation in response to both lysosomal and mitochondrial dysfunction.

claims.claim: The constitutive silencing of the pseudo-hypoxia response requires both functional lysosomes and functional mitochondria.
claims.source: Reciprocally, it can also be noted that the constitutive silencing of the (pseudo)hypoxia response requires both functional lysosomes and functional mitochondria.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the data showing HIF-1α accumulation when either lysosomes or mitochondria are dysfunctional.

claims.claim: Many genes causing inherited Parkinson's disease are associated with mitochondria or lysosomes/autophagy.
claims.source: For example, many of the genes that cause inherited Parkinson's disease are associated either with mitochondria or lysosomes/autophagy, and therefore the primarily-damaged organelle is likely to promote the secondary impairment of the other.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: This manuscript presents a novel role of mitochondria-lysosome crosstalk in the regulation of central nervous system inflammation in vivo.
claims.source: This manuscript presents a novel role of mitochondria-lysosome crosstalk in the regulation of central nervous system inflammation in vivo.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by the comprehensive data showing the link between lysosomal dysfunction, iron deficiency, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation in Gaa-KO mice.

results.result: Inhibition of lysosomal acidification by v-ATPase inhibitors (bafilomycin and saliphenylhalamide) triggers cellular iron deficiency. This is demonstrated by decreased total, Fe2+, and Fe3+ levels in the cytoplasm, increased lysosomal iron retention, increased Tfrc transcript levels, decreased ferritin protein levels, and decreased FerroOrange signal. Fe-citrate supplementation deactivates this iron-deficiency response.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C15-C22, and C118 collectively demonstrate that v-ATPase inhibition causes iron retention in lysosomes and cytoplasmic iron deficiency through multiple complementary measurements (iron assays, gene expression, protein levels, and fluorescent probes). The rescue by Fe-citrate supplementation (C22) provides strong evidence that the effect is specifically due to impaired iron release from lysosomes.

results.result: v-ATPase inhibition leads to HIF-1α accumulation and activation of HIF-1α target genes, which is reversed by Fe-citrate supplementation. VHL protein levels remain unchanged, and α-ketoglutarate supplementation does not prevent HIF-1α accumulation, indicating that iron deficiency is the primary cause of HIF-1α stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14 and C23-C27 demonstrate HIF-1α accumulation upon v-ATPase inhibition through immunoblots and show that this is not due to VHL changes or α-ketoglutarate deficiency. The rescue by Fe-citrate (C23-C27) and induction of HIF-1α target genes provide strong mechanistic evidence linking iron deficiency to HIF-1α stabilization.

results.result: Genetic silencing of Atp6v1h, a v-ATPase subunit, recapitulates the iron deficiency phenotype observed with pharmacological v-ATPase inhibition, including impaired lysosomal acidification, increased Tfrc expression, decreased ferritin levels, HIF-1α accumulation, and increased HIF-1α target gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 demonstrate that genetic perturbation of v-ATPase produces the same iron deficiency and HIF-1α phenotypes as pharmacological inhibition, strengthening the conclusion that lysosomal acidification is required for iron homeostasis. The consistency across multiple readouts provides robust support.

results.result: Gaa-KO fibroblasts, which have impaired lysosomal acidification due to loss of acid α-glucosidase, exhibit iron deficiency characterized by increased Tfrc expression, decreased FTL1 levels, HIF-1α accumulation, decreased Fe2+, and increased Fe3+. The increase in Fe3+ suggests a defect in endolysosomal reduction of Fe3+ to Fe2+.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C37 demonstrate that a genetic model of impaired lysosomal acidification (Gaa-KO) produces iron deficiency phenotypes consistent with pharmacological and siRNA-mediated v-ATPase inhibition. The observation of increased Fe3+ (C37) provides mechanistic insight into the role of acidic pH in iron reduction by STEAP3.

results.result: Iron deficiency caused by lysosomal acidification impairment results in impaired mitochondrial function, including decreased mitochondrial Fe2+ levels, decreased oxygen consumption, decreased protein and transcript levels of respiratory chain subunits, decreased mitochondrial mass markers, and mitochondrial fragmentation. Fe-citrate supplementation restores mitochondrial function.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C38-C52 provide comprehensive evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction through multiple complementary assays (Mito-FerroGreen staining, Seahorse respirometry, Western blots, qPCR, microscopy). The rescue by Fe-citrate supplementation (C39, C43-C45, C51-C52) demonstrates that iron deficiency is the primary cause of mitochondrial dysfunction.

results.result: v-ATPase inhibition leads to increased mitochondrial superoxide levels, increased reactive oxygen species, and increased lipid peroxidation, all of which are recovered by Fe-citrate supplementation.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 demonstrate oxidative stress resulting from iron deficiency-induced mitochondrial dysfunction using multiple complementary probes (MitoSox, DCF, BODIPY C11). The rescue by Fe-citrate supplementation provides strong evidence that oxidative stress is a consequence of iron deficiency.

results.result: Atp6v1h-silenced fibroblasts show decreased mitochondrial respiratory chain activity, decreased protein levels of OXPHOS subunits, and decreased mitochondrial biogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 demonstrate that genetic perturbation of v-ATPase produces mitochondrial dysfunction consistent with pharmacological inhibition, supporting the conclusion that lysosomal acidification is required for mitochondrial function.

results.result: Loss of lysosomal iron exporters Mcoln1 and/or Slc11a2 triggers iron deficiency (increased Tfrc, decreased FTL1) and mitochondrial dysfunction (decreased respiration, decreased OXPHOS protein and transcript levels), demonstrating that iron retention in lysosomes is sufficient to cause these phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C70 provide strong evidence that blocking lysosomal iron export, independent of acidification, is sufficient to cause iron deficiency and mitochondrial dysfunction. This supports the model that iron release from lysosomes is critical for cellular iron homeostasis and mitochondrial function.

results.result: v-ATPase inhibition causes non-apoptotic cell death that is rescued by Fe-citrate supplementation. The cell death is not prevented by pan-caspase inhibitor ZVAD, necrostatin-1s, or ferrostatin, and shows no cleaved caspase-3 or cleaved PARP. Antimycin A treatment abolishes the rescue by iron supplementation, indicating that mitochondrial respiratory chain activity is required for the protective effect of iron.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C71-C82, C126-C127 demonstrate that v-ATPase inhibition causes cell death that is rescued by iron supplementation and requires mitochondrial function. The characterization of the cell death as non-apoptotic, non-necroptotic, and non-ferroptotic is supported by multiple negative controls with specific inhibitors.

results.result: Iron deficiency induced by deferoxamine treatment is sufficient to trigger inflammatory signaling in cultured primary neurons, including increased expression of Tnfa, innate immune regulators (Tlr9, Myd88, Irf7, Stat1, Stat2), and interferon-stimulated genes (Cxcl10, Isg15, Ifit1, Ifit3, Ifi44). The inflammation trigger appears to be cell-intrinsic.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C83-C85, and C129 demonstrate that iron deficiency alone is sufficient to trigger inflammatory gene expression in neurons. The use of deferoxamine, which chelates iron without directly affecting v-ATPase or autophagy, provides strong evidence for a direct link between iron deficiency and inflammation.

results.result: The Gaa-KO mouse model shows a robust iron deficiency response in the brain at 6 and 12 months of age, including increased Tfrc transcript levels, decreased FTL1 protein levels, HIF-1α accumulation, decreased complex IV activity, decreased T2 relaxation times by MRI, reduced choline-containing compounds by MRS, and decreased myelination-related proteins (PLP and MBP).
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C86-C92 provide comprehensive in vivo evidence of iron deficiency in the Gaa-KO brain using multiple complementary approaches (qPCR, Western blot, enzyme activity assays, MRI, MRS). The MRI data (C90) provides non-invasive verification of iron deficiency in living animals.

results.result: The brains of Gaa-KO mice present a pervasive inflammatory signature at 2, 6, and 12 months of age, characterized by enrichment of inflammation-related pathways, activation of Irf7 and Irf3 transcription factors, increased expression of interferon-stimulated genes, and increased GFAP levels indicating glial activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C93-C101 provide comprehensive evidence of inflammation in the Gaa-KO brain using unbiased RNA sequencing, pathway analysis, qPCR validation, and immunohistochemistry. The early onset (2 months) and progressive nature of the inflammatory response are well-documented.

results.result: Iron deficiency is associated with mtDNA instability in multiple models, including Gaa-KO mice (age-dependent decline in mtDNA copy number and reduced TFAM protein levels), deferoxamine-treated cells and neurons, Irp1/2-KO fibroblasts, and Gaa-KO fibroblasts. The decrease in TFAM protein levels cannot be fully explained by decreased transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C102-C109, C133-C134 demonstrate a consistent association between iron deficiency and mtDNA instability across multiple cell types and experimental models. The observation that TFAM protein levels are more severely affected than transcript levels (C104) suggests post-transcriptional regulation.

results.result: Iron supplementation (Fe-citrate in cells, iron-enriched diet in mice) corrects the inflammatory signature, mtDNA instability, and motor deficits in Gaa-KO models. In 2-month-old Gaa-KO mice, iron-enriched diet rescues mtDNA copy number, dampens inflammatory gene expression, reduces GFAP and TNFα protein levels, normalizes cytokine levels, and normalizes stride length.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C110-C115, and C137 provide strong evidence that iron supplementation is sufficient to rescue multiple phenotypes in Gaa-KO models, including mtDNA instability, inflammation, and motor deficits. The comprehensive rescue across multiple readouts supports the conclusion that iron deficiency is the primary driver of these phenotypes.

results.result: Supplying iron via a lysosome-independent pathway (Fe-citrate supplementation) recovers the effects of lysosomal acidification inhibition in cultured cells, including restoration of HIF-1α levels, ferritin levels, HIF-1α target gene expression, mitochondrial Fe2+ levels, mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial gene expression, mitochondrial superoxide levels, ROS levels, lipid peroxidation, and cell viability.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and related rescue experiments (C22-C24, C27, C39, C43-C45, C51-C52, C54, C56, C58, C73) provide comprehensive evidence that bypassing the lysosomal pathway with Fe-citrate is sufficient to rescue all major phenotypes caused by v-ATPase inhibition. This strongly supports the conclusion that iron deficiency is the primary mechanism underlying these phenotypes.

results.result: The manuscript presents a novel mechanism linking impaired lysosomal acidification to mitochondrial malfunction and inflammation in vivo. Iron release from lysosomes requires acidic pH for STEAP3-mediated Fe3+ reduction to Fe2+, which can then be exported via DMT1 or MCOLN1. Cytoplasmic iron levels regulate the iron deficiency response through IRP1/IRP2. Iron deficiency impairs mtDNA synthesis (via ribonucleotide reductase) and HIF-1α degradation (via prolyl hydroxylases), leading to mtDNA instability, inflammation, and cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C147 synthesize the mechanistic model supported by the experimental data. The model is well-supported by the comprehensive evidence showing that: (1) lysosomal acidification is required for iron release, (2) iron deficiency causes mitochondrial dysfunction and mtDNA instability, (3) mtDNA instability triggers inflammation, and (4) iron supplementation rescues all phenotypes. The integration of established knowledge (C120-C124, C130-C132, C135, C138-C141, C143, C146) with novel findings is appropriate.

results.result: Decreased stride length in Gaa-KO mice is an indication of gait disorder, suggesting motor impairments.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is supported by citation to Fernagut et al., 2002, and the DigiGait data showing decreased stride length in Gaa-KO mice (C115). However, the interpretation is somewhat inferential as the manuscript does not provide extensive behavioral characterization beyond stride length.
